# Introduction

hakobu runs your projects on servers you own. A project says what it needs in a file in its repository, `hakobu.toml`; CI builds each commit into images; the server pulls the new release and swaps it in with no downtime, then tells the commit how it went. There's no panel and no database: the file is the state, and the code that keeps your data safe (deploys, backups, secrets, alerts) is written and tested once, in hakobu.

## What it does

- **Deploys by pull.** CI pushes a release image; the server checks its tag every 30 seconds and deploys a new one. Nothing connects to the server from outside, and any CI that can push an image works. The commit gets a `hakobu/deploy` status, and the CI job waits for it, so a failed deploy is a red commit with the reason.
- **Safe deploys.** Before a deploy with migrations, hakobu dumps the databases; migrations run in the new image, and if they fail, the running version stays. The new version takes traffic only once it answers its health check. A deploy never deletes data: what the file no longer has is kept until a person deletes it.
- **Databases and caches.** PostgreSQL databases with their own users, and Valkey (Redis-compatible) caches, with passwords made on the server and handed to the apps as variables.
- **Secrets in the repository**, each sealed with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to the server and to you: anyone, an agent too, can add one; only the server and you can read them.
- **Backups** of every database and volume each day, sealed, to any S3 bucket and a copy elsewhere, each restored into scratch right after upload to prove it restores.
- **Alerts** by email when an app is down, a deploy or backup fails, the disk fills, or the audit finds a port open to the internet or a container hakobu didn't start; a pulse to a dead man's switch says hakobu itself is alive.
- **Agents welcome.** `hakobu init` gives a repository a skill for Claude Code that says how to change the file and migrations safely, and the `hakobu mcp` server lets an agent see status and logs, deploy and roll back. Deleting or restoring data is a person's to do, and the agent can't.

## What it needs

- A Linux server (Debian or Ubuntu, amd64 or arm64) with systemd. The installer sets up rootless Docker and Tailscale.
- A [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) tailnet: hakobu's API listens there and nowhere else.
- A registry for the images (GitHub's ghcr.io works with no setup) and a CI to build them (the workflow hakobu provides is for GitHub Actions).
- For backups, an S3 bucket (Cloudflare R2, Hetzner Object Storage, AWS, any other); for alerts, an SMTP account.
- For the web, either ports 80 and 443 (hakobu gets Let's Encrypt certificates) or a Cloudflare Tunnel.

hakobu calls no provider's API: no DNS, no cloud, no Git host beyond the commit status. What's different in each project (its file, Dockerfile, migrations, DNS records) is for you or your agent to write.

Start with [a server](https://hakobu.dev/docs/install/index.md), then [a project](https://hakobu.dev/docs/project/index.md).

# A server

One command sets a server up, and asks nothing: everything comes from the environment, so cloud-init or an agent can run it.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://hakobu.dev/install.sh | sudo \
  HAKOBU_NAME=kasl-1 \
  HAKOBU_OWNER_KEY=age1… \
  TS_AUTHKEY=tskey-auth-… TS_TAGS=tag:hakobu \
  HAKOBU_INGRESS=public HAKOBU_ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com \
  bash
```

It installs rootless Docker (as the user `hakobu-docker`), Tailscale, unattended upgrades, hakobu (its signature checked) as a sandboxed systemd service running as `hakobu`, writes `/etc/hakobu/server.toml` and makes the server's key. Run it again to update: the config, the key and the data stay.

## Before you start

- **Your key.** `age-keygen` makes one; keep the secret half in your password manager and give the public half (`age1…`) as `HAKOBU_OWNER_KEY`. Every secret and backup is sealed to it as well as to the server, so you can open them if the server is gone.
- **A Tailscale auth key** ([admin console](https://login.tailscale.com/admin/settings/keys)), with the tag you'll give the server. The API listens only on the server's tailnet address. Your tailnet's policy should let your devices reach the tag on port 7070, and nothing else need reach it.

## Settings

| Variable | |
|---|---|
| `HAKOBU_NAME` | the server's name: lowercase letters, digits and `-` |
| `HAKOBU_OWNER_KEY` | your age public key |
| `TS_AUTHKEY` | a Tailscale auth key, unless the server is in the tailnet already |
| `TS_TAGS` | the server's Tailscale tags, `tag:hakobu` say |
| `HAKOBU_INGRESS` | `public`, `tunnel` or `none` (the default): see below |
| `HAKOBU_ACME_EMAIL` | Let's Encrypt's contact, for `public` |
| `CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN` | the tunnel's token, for `tunnel` |
| `HAKOBU_CONFIG_EXTRA` | a file whose TOML goes at the end of the config: releases, registries, backups, alerts (see [Server config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md)) |
| `HAKOBU_VERSION` | a release; default the newest |

## How the web gets in

- **`public`**: hakobu answers ports 80 and 443 itself, with a Let's Encrypt certificate for each app's domain (and only those). Point each domain's DNS at the server.
- **`tunnel`**: cloudflared runs on the server with your tunnel's token and sends requests to hakobu on loopback; the server needs no open port. In Cloudflare, route each domain of the tunnel to `http://localhost:8080`.
- **`none`**: apps aren't served to the web; for a server of workers only, or while you set it up.

## The tokens

On a first install it prints two tokens, once:

- the **operator** token, for your laptop and your agent: status, logs, deploy, rollback, backup;
- the **admin** token, for your password manager only: it alone can restore and delete data.

On your laptop, with the hakobu binary from the [releases](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu/releases):

```bash
hakobu server add kasl-1 http://100.x.y.z:7070   # then paste the operator token
hakobu status
```

The installer's output names the API's address. Servers are remembered in `~/.config/hakobu/servers.toml`.

## Back up the server's key

`/var/lib/hakobu/key.age` opens the server's secrets and backups. Your own key does too, so losing the server's isn't fatal, but a copy off the server spares you re-sealing secrets on a new one.

# A project

A project is a repository with a `hakobu.toml` at its root. In the repository, with a [server](https://hakobu.dev/docs/install/index.md) added:

```bash
hakobu init --server kasl-1
```

It writes, leaving any file that's already there:

- **`hakobu.toml`**, with an app for each directory (the root and one level down) that has a Dockerfile, or a stack it recognizes (Node, Python, Go, …), marked as needing a Dockerfile: hakobu builds each app from its own;
- **`.github/workflows/hakobu.yml`**, which builds each push to the default branch and waits for its deploy;
- **`.claude/skills/hakobu/SKILL.md`**, a section in **`CLAUDE.md`**, **`.mcp.json`** and **`.claude/settings.json`**: see [Agents](https://hakobu.dev/docs/agents/index.md).

The image goes to `ghcr.io/OWNER/REPO` (from `origin`); `--image` gives another.

## Then

1. **The file.** Give each app its `domain`, a `health` path it answers once it's ready (`/up` by default), and the databases and caches it uses: see [hakobu.toml](https://hakobu.dev/docs/hakobu-toml/index.md). `hakobu validate` checks it.
2. **Secrets.** `hakobu secret init` starts `hakobu.secrets.toml`, sealed to the server's key and yours. Add the token that lets the server set the commit's status, a [fine-grained token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) with **Commit statuses: Read and write** on this repository alone:

   ```bash
   hakobu secret set hakobu status_token
   ```

   and your app's own secrets with `hakobu secret set APP NAME`. See [Secrets](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md).
3. **The server** needs to know the release image, and to be allowed to pull it. In its `/etc/hakobu/server.toml`, then `sudo systemctl restart hakobu`:

   ```toml
   releases = ["ghcr.io/kasl/crm:main"]

   [registries."ghcr.io"]
   username = "kasl"
   password = "github_pat_…"   # a token that may read the packages
   ```

   See [Server config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md).
4. **Push.** CI builds the apps, pushes them and the release; within 30 seconds the server deploys it, and the job turns green once it's live. `hakobu status` and `hakobu deploys` show it from your laptop.

## An arm64 server

Images are built on CI's runner, for its architecture. For an arm64 server, set `runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm` in the workflow.

## Tests first

The workflow is a job like any other: put your tests in a job of their own and add `needs: [test]` to the deploy job.

# hakobu.toml

What a project's server runs, at the root of its repository. It's strict: an unknown key, a typo or a reference to nothing is an error, so a mistake stops the deploy instead of quietly turning something off. `hakobu validate` checks it, and CI runs it before each build.

```toml
project = "crm"
server = "kasl-1"

[apps.web]
domain = "crm.example.com"
release = "bin/rails db:migrate"
worker = "bin/jobs"
uses = ["main", "cache"]
volumes = { uploads = "/rails/storage" }
env = { RAILS_LOG_LEVEL = "info" }

[apps.admin]
path = "admin"
domain = "admin.crm.example.com"
uses = ["main"]

[databases.main]

[caches.cache]
memory = "128mb"
```

Names (the project's, apps', databases', caches', volumes') are lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter, up to 31 characters.

## The project

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `project` | the project's name, unique on its server |
| `server` | the server it deploys to; any other server refuses the release |

One repository is one project.

## Apps: `[apps.NAME]`

An app is one image serving HTTP, and optionally a worker from the same image.

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `path` | its directory in the repository, default the root; the app is built from the `Dockerfile` there |
| `domain` | where it's served on the web; without one, it isn't |
| `health` | a path that answers 2xx once the app takes requests; default `/up`. A deploy goes live only once it does |
| `port` | the port it listens on; default the image's `EXPOSE`, else 8080. It's in `$PORT` too |
| `release` | a command run once per deploy in the new image before it takes traffic, for migrations: if it fails, the running version stays. See [Deploys](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md) |
| `worker` | the command of a background process from the same image |
| `memory` | its limit, `512mb` or `1gb`; at least `64mb` |
| `cpus` | its CPU limit, `0.5` or `2` |
| `volumes` | name → mount path. Survives deploys and is backed up |
| `env` | variables, plain values only: secrets go in [hakobu.secrets.toml](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) |
| `uses` | the databases and caches it uses: a list, or a map of name → prefix |

The app must listen on all interfaces (not only 127.0.0.1). `release` and `worker` run with `/bin/sh -c` in its image, which therefore needs a shell.

### `uses`

A database gives the app `DATABASE_URL`, `POSTGRES_HOST`, `POSTGRES_PORT`, `POSTGRES_DB`, `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`; a cache `REDIS_URL`, `VALKEY_URL`, `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT` and `REDIS_PASSWORD`. Two of a kind would set the same variables, so give one a prefix:

```toml
uses = { main = "", jobs = "JOBS" }   # JOBS_REDIS_URL, JOBS_REDIS_HOST, …
```

### Volumes

An app with volumes is stopped before its new version starts, so two versions never write the same files: a few seconds down on each deploy. The worker shares them.

## Databases: `[databases.NAME]`

A database and its own user on the server's PostgreSQL, which all its projects share; its version is the server's. It has no keys. See [Databases](https://hakobu.dev/docs/databases/index.md).

## Caches: `[caches.NAME]`

A Valkey server of the project's own, with its own password.

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `memory` | its memory, default `256mb`, at least `16mb` |

## What a change does

- **Adding** an app, database, cache or volume makes it on the next deploy.
- **Removing** one doesn't delete it: a database, cache or volume is kept, *orphaned*, and only `hakobu destroy` (a person's, with the admin token, after a last backup) deletes it.
- **Renaming** is removing and adding: the new one starts empty and the old one is orphaned. For a database, the deploy stops instead and says so: deploy the new one, move the data, then take the old one out.

# Secrets

An app's secrets live in its repository, in `hakobu.secrets.toml` next to `hakobu.toml`, each value sealed on its own with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to two keys: the server's and yours. Anyone with the repository can add or replace a secret, an agent too; only the server and you can read one. The file is committed like any other, and its diffs show which secret changed, never a value.

## Commands

```bash
hakobu secret init               # start the file, sealed to the server's key and yours
hakobu secret set web STRIPE_KEY # read from stdin (or typed, hidden): never an argument
hakobu secret list               # names only
hakobu secret unset web STRIPE_KEY
```

`hakobu secret init` asks the server for its public key; after that, sealing needs no server. `set` reads the value from stdin so it stays out of your shell's history:

```bash
op read op://crm/stripe/key | hakobu secret set web STRIPE_KEY
```

An app gets its secrets as variables. A secret can't have the name of one the file already sets (in `env`, from `uses`, or `PORT`): the server refuses that release rather than guess which wins.

## hakobu's own

`APP` `hakobu` is for hakobu itself. `status_token` is the GitHub token that sets the commit's `hakobu/deploy` status: a [fine-grained token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) with **Commit statuses: Read and write** on the repository alone. A release from a GitHub repository without it is refused, so a deploy is never silent.

## How they reach the server

CI puts the file, still sealed, in the release image; the server opens it with its key as it deploys. A [rollback](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md) takes the older image but today's secrets, so a rotated key stays rotated.

Database and cache passwords aren't secrets you keep: the server makes them.

## A new server

A new server has a new key, which can't open what was sealed to the old one. Put the old server's key back from your copy of `/var/lib/hakobu/key.age`, or start the file anew for the new server and set each secret again (`hakobu secret list` names them).

# Deploys and CI

Nothing pushes to a server. CI builds each commit into a **release image** and pushes it to a registry under a tag (`main`); the server checks that tag every 30 seconds and deploys each new one. CI needs no access to the server, and the server no inbound connection.

## The release image

`hakobu build`, which the workflow runs, builds each app of `hakobu.toml` from the Dockerfile in its directory, pushes it as `IMAGE-APP`, then pushes the release last: a tiny image whose labels carry `hakobu.toml`, the sealed `hakobu.secrets.toml`, each app's image pinned by digest, and the repository and commit it came from. The release goes last, so a server never sees one whose apps aren't pushed yet. Every app of a commit deploys together.

## A deploy

1. **Plan**: the file against what runs. A wrong file, a secret the server can't open or a renamed database stops here, before anything changes.
2. **A dump** of each database the app uses, if it has a `release` command.
3. **`release`** in the new image, with the app's variables. If it fails, the deploy stops and the running version goes on.
4. **The new version** starts, next to the old one, and must answer its `health` path with 2xx.
5. **Traffic switches** to it; the old version stops. No request is dropped (an app with volumes is the exception: it stops first, see [volumes](https://hakobu.dev/docs/hakobu-toml/index.md)).

A deploy never deletes data: databases, caches and volumes gone from the file are kept, orphaned.

## The commit status

The server sets the commit's `hakobu/deploy` status: pending as it starts, then success, or failure with the reason. The workflow's `hakobu wait` waits for it (15 minutes by default), so the CI job fails when the deploy does. Without the [status token](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) the release is refused.

The failure email, `hakobu deploys` and `hakobu logs PROJECT/APP` say more.

## Migrations

`release` runs while the old version still serves, and if anything after it fails, the old version goes on against the migrated database. So a migration must work with the code before it:

- add columns nullable or with a default, and tables, freely;
- rename or drop in two deploys: first stop using the column, then drop it;
- don't change a column's type in place: add another and backfill;
- long backfills belong in the worker, not `release` (it's stopped after 30 minutes).

## Rollback

```bash
hakobu rollback crm
```

deploys the release before the current one, with today's secrets, and holds the current one back until a newer one comes. It doesn't undo migrations: the dump taken before the last deploy stays on the server, in `/var/lib/hakobu/snapshots`, and `hakobu restore` puts back a [backup](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md). `hakobu deploy crm` checks for a release now instead of in 30 seconds; `--force` deploys the current one again.

## The workflow

`hakobu init` writes `.github/workflows/hakobu.yml`, which calls `hakobudev/hakobu/.github/workflows/build.yml` with:

| Input | |
|---|---|
| `version` | the hakobu release to build with; the same as the workflow's ref |
| `image` | the release image, without its tag; default `ghcr.io/OWNER/REPO` |
| `tag` | the tag the server polls; default `main` |
| `runner` | the runner, whose architecture the images get; `ubuntu-24.04-arm` for an arm64 server |
| `wait` | how long to wait for the deploy; default `15m` |

For a registry other than ghcr.io, pass `registry-username` and `registry-password` as secrets. Releases run one at a time per repository, each waiting for its deploy.

Another CI works the same way: run `hakobu build --image IMAGE --tag main` where it can push, then `hakobu wait` (it reads GitHub's statuses, so it needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` and the commit).

# Databases

`[databases.NAME]` in [hakobu.toml](https://hakobu.dev/docs/hakobu-toml/index.md) is a PostgreSQL database with its own user, in the server's one PostgreSQL, which every project on the server shares. Only the apps that `use` it get its address and password; the password is made on the server.

```toml
[apps.web]
uses = ["main"]

[databases.main]
```

The app gets `DATABASE_URL` (`postgres://…`), `POSTGRES_HOST`, `POSTGRES_PORT`, `POSTGRES_DB`, `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`; with a prefix (`uses = { main = "APP" }`), `APP_DATABASE_URL` and so on.

## Its version

The PostgreSQL image is the one this hakobu release pins, for every project on the server: a database has no version of its own.

## Shared memory

PostgreSQL keeps the memory of parallel queries, hashes and sorts in `/dev/shm`, of which Docker gives a container 64 MB, too little for a large query (`could not resize shared memory segment … No space left on device`). hakobu gives PostgreSQL a quarter of the server's memory, up to 1 GB; it's memory only while a query uses it.

## Migrations

Run them as the app's `release` command, and keep them backward compatible: see [Deploys](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md). Before each deploy with a `release`, the databases the app uses are dumped on the server.

## Backups

Every database is backed up daily, sealed, checked by a restore into scratch, and kept 7 days plus 4 weeks: see [Backups and recovery](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md).

## Deleting one

Removing it from the file keeps it, orphaned. `hakobu destroy PROJECT/NAME` deletes it after a last backup, with the admin token, at a terminal, typing its name to confirm.

# Agents (Claude Code, MCP)

hakobu is built so an agent can do the work that's different in each project (the file, the Dockerfile, migrations, DNS) while the parts that guard your data stay in tested code it can't change. `hakobu init` sets a repository up for that.

## The skill

`.claude/skills/hakobu/SKILL.md` tells Claude Code how deploys work, how to write `hakobu.toml`, that migrations must work with the version before, how to add secrets without reading them, and what not to do. `hakobu init` writes it anew each time, so it matches the hakobu you run; a short section in `CLAUDE.md` points to it.

## MCP

`.mcp.json` adds hakobu's MCP server, `hakobu mcp`, which runs on your laptop and talks to every server you've added, with the operator token. Its tools: `status`, `deploys`, `logs`, `backups`, `deploy`, `rollback` and `backup`. For another client, add it as a local (stdio) server running `hakobu mcp`.

## What an agent can't do

- **Delete or replace data.** `hakobu destroy` and `hakobu restore` need the admin token, which belongs in your password manager, and a person at a terminal typing a confirmation: without a terminal they refuse. `.claude/settings.json` denies both to Claude Code as well. The MCP server has neither.
- **Read a secret.** It can seal a new one to the server, never open one. The skill tells it to ask you to run `hakobu secret set`.
- **Reach the server.** No SSH is needed for any of this, and the API is on your tailnet only.

The logs an agent reads are written by your apps, and text in them could try to steer it; what it can do with the operator token is bounded the same either way.

# Server config

A server is configured in `/etc/hakobu/server.toml`, readable by hakobu alone. The installer writes the first part; the rest you add (or pass to the installer as `HAKOBU_CONFIG_EXTRA`), then `sudo systemctl restart hakobu`. Like `hakobu.toml`, it's strict: an unknown key stops hakobu from starting, and `journalctl -u hakobu` says why.

```toml
name = "kasl-1"
listen = "100.101.102.103:7070"
owner_key = "age1…"
operator_token_sha256 = "…"
admin_token_sha256 = "…"

releases = ["ghcr.io/kasl/crm:main", "ghcr.io/kasl/site:main"]

[registries."ghcr.io"]
username = "kasl"
password = "github_pat_…"

[ingress]
mode = "public"
email = "you@example.com"

[backups]
at = "03:00"
[backups.primary]
endpoint = "https://ACCOUNT.r2.cloudflarestorage.com"
region = "auto"
bucket = "kasl-backups"
access_key = "…"
secret_key = "…"
[[backups.copies]]
name = "hetzner"
endpoint = "https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com"
region = "fsn1"
bucket = "kasl-backups-copy"
access_key = "…"   # a key that can only write
secret_key = "…"

[alerts]
pulse_url = "https://hc-ping.com/…"
pulse_fail_url = "https://hc-ping.com/…/fail"
allow_ports = [22]
[alerts.smtp]
host = "smtp.example.com"
port = 465
username = "…"
password = "…"
from = "hakobu@example.com"
to = "you@example.com"
```

## Keys

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the server's name; a project's `server` must match it |
| `listen` | the API's address, on the tailnet; an address on every interface is refused |
| `data_dir` | default `/var/lib/hakobu`: the key, state, deploy history, dumps |
| `owner_key` | your age public key |
| `operator_token_sha256`, `admin_token_sha256` | the tokens' SHA-256 (`hakobu server token` makes a new pair) |
| `releases` | the release images to deploy, one a project, by tag |
| `poll_every` | how often to check them; default `30s` |
| `registries."HOST"` | `username` and `password` to pull from a registry |
| `ingress` | `mode` (`public` or `tunnel`), `email` (Let's Encrypt's contact), `listen` (for `tunnel`, on loopback; default `127.0.0.1:8080`) |
| `backups` | `at` (UTC, default `03:00`), `keep_daily` (7), `keep_weekly` (4), `primary` and `copies`: see [Backups](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md) |
| `alerts` | `smtp`, `pulse_url`, `pulse_fail_url`, `allow_ports`: see [Alerts](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md) |

A bucket has `endpoint`, `region`, `bucket`, `access_key`, `secret_key`, and `prefix` (default `hakobu/NAME/`); copies have a `name`.

## Tailscale

The API listens on the server's tailnet address only. In your tailnet's policy, let your own devices reach the server's tag on port 7070; nothing else needs to. The installer leaves Tailscale's SSH, routes and DNS off.

## From your laptop

```bash
hakobu server add kasl-1 http://100.101.102.103:7070   # the operator token on stdin
hakobu server list
hakobu status              # every server
hakobu --server kasl-1 deploys
```

# Backups and recovery

With a bucket in the [server's config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md), every database and volume on the server is backed up each day at `backups.at` (UTC). Caches aren't: they're caches.

## Each backup is

- **sealed** with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to the server's key and to yours, so the bucket alone reads nothing, and you can open a backup without the server;
- **copied**: written to the primary bucket and to each of `backups.copies`, another provider ideally, with a key that may only write, so a leaked key of the server can't delete the copies;
- **proved**: read back from the primary bucket and restored into scratch (a database counts its tables, a volume's archive is read through) before it counts as done;
- **rotated**: the last 7 days and one a week for 4 weeks are kept (`keep_daily`, `keep_weekly`). A bucket with object lock may refuse a deletion; it's tried again on the next rotation.

There's no catalog to lose: the backups are listed from the primary bucket itself.

A volume's app and worker are paused for the seconds the archive takes, so files that belong together (SQLite and its journal) are copied as of one moment.

A failed or unproved backup emails you (see [Alerts](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md)).

## Commands

```bash
hakobu backup              # back up everything now
hakobu backups crm         # list, newest first, with what reading each back found
```

## Restoring

```bash
hakobu restore crm/main               # a database, from its newest backup
hakobu restore crm/web/uploads --at 2026-10-20T03:00:12Z
```

A restore replaces the data, so it needs the admin token (from `HAKOBU_ADMIN_TOKEN` or typed, hidden) and a person at a terminal: an agent can't run it. The database or volume must exist on the server (deploy the project first).

## Before each deploy

A deploy with a `release` command first dumps the databases its app uses, on the server, in `/var/lib/hakobu/snapshots`: the state just before a migration, if it goes wrong.

# Alerts and audit

The server watches itself and emails you through any SMTP server (`[alerts.smtp]` in its [config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md)): one email when a problem starts and one when it's over, never a stream. Without SMTP, problems show only in `hakobu status`.

## What it watches

- an app that hasn't answered its health check for 3 minutes;
- a failed deploy (closed by the next one that works) or backup, and a backup that didn't prove it restores;
- the disk 85% full (closed under 80%);
- PostgreSQL not answering;
- the **audit**, hourly:
  - a port listening beyond loopback and the tailnet that isn't in `alerts.allow_ports` (80 and 443 are allowed for `public` ingress by themselves; add 22 if SSH listens on every address);
  - a container hakobu didn't start;
  - unattended upgrades that haven't run for 3 days.

What's fixed closes by itself. Problems survive a restart of hakobu, so you aren't mailed twice.

The audit sees what listens on the machine, not a firewall in front of it (a cloud firewall is outside its view), and only TCP.

## The pulse

Every 15 minutes hakobu fetches `alerts.pulse_url`, or `alerts.pulse_fail_url` while a problem is open. Point them at a dead man's switch ([healthchecks.io](https://healthchecks.io) and the like): it emails you when the pulses stop, which is how you hear that hakobu, or the whole server, is down.

## Your apps' errors

hakobu doesn't collect errors or traces. Give an app a `SENTRY_DSN` [secret](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) and any Sentry-compatible service has them.

# Updates

To update a server, run the installer again, with the version if you want a particular one:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://hakobu.dev/install.sh | sudo HAKOBU_VERSION=v1.0.0 bash
```

The config, the key and the data stay. Apps keep running; their proxies live in hakobu, so they don't answer for about half a second while it restarts. Docker is restarted only if its settings changed.

The CLI on your laptop is the binary from the [release](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu/releases), and a project's workflow names its version (`version:` and the ref of `uses:`): bump both together.

## Signed releases

Releases are signed with an Ed25519 key that never leaves the release workflow. The installer and the workflow install a release only if its signature over `hakobu <version>` and its checksums is by that key, so neither a tampered download nor an older release under a newer name gets in.

# Security

What hakobu does to keep your apps and data yours, and what it doesn't promise.

## Nothing comes in

The server pulls its releases; no CI, panel or agent connects to it. hakobu's API listens on the tailnet only (an address on every interface is refused), and the web reaches apps only through 80/443 for their own domains, or a Cloudflare Tunnel with no port open at all. The [audit](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md) emails you about any other port that listens.

## Two tokens

The **operator** token (laptop, agent) can look, deploy, roll back and back up. The **admin** token alone can restore or delete data; keep it in your password manager. The server keeps only their SHA-256. Restore and destroy also need a person at a terminal typing a confirmation, and delete only what the file no longer has, after a last backup.

## Isolation

hakobu runs as the unprivileged `hakobu` user, in a sandboxed systemd unit, and [rootless Docker](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/rootless/) as another, `hakobu-docker`: neither a break-in into hakobu nor a container escape gets root, and an escape can't read hakobu's data. Containers run with `no-new-privileges` and without raw sockets. Each project has its own Docker network; each database its own PostgreSQL user, and each cache its own server and password.

## Secrets and backups

Sealed with age to the server's key and yours: see [Secrets](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) and [Backups](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md). The repository, the registry and the backup buckets hold nothing readable without one of the two keys. Backup copies go with a key that may only write.

## What's beyond it

The release image is trusted as it comes: whoever can push to its tag deploys to the server. Guard the registry, and CI's ability to push, as you would SSH. A malicious app can read its own secrets and its own databases, as any app can.

## Releases

Signed, and installed only after checking the signature: see [Updates](https://hakobu.dev/docs/updates/index.md).

## Reporting a problem

Found a vulnerability? Please report it privately through [GitHub's security advisories](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu/security/advisories/new) rather than in an issue.

# Development

hakobu is open source under the MIT license: [github.com/hakobudev/hakobu](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu).

## Building

```bash
go build -o hakobu .
```

Requires Go 1.27+. The server side needs Linux, systemd and Docker; `install.sh` with `HAKOBU_BINARY=./hakobu` installs a local build on a test machine.

## Tests

`just check` runs what CI runs: build, vet, tests, govulncheck and golangci-lint. Tests that need Docker (they start their own containers: PostgreSQL, Valkey, an S3 server) run with `HAKOBU_DOCKER_TEST=1 go test ./internal/apply ./internal/backups`.

## These docs

The pages of hakobu.dev/docs are made from `docs/*.md` (the menu is `docs/nav.md`) by `go run ./tools/docsgen` into `site/docs/`; a test fails when they're behind the Markdown.

## Releases

Pushing a `vX.Y.Z` tag builds and publishes a release (`.github/workflows/release.yml`), signed with the key in the `HAKOBU_SIGNING_KEY` secret of the `release` environment; without it the release fails rather than going out unsigned. `just release-check` builds a snapshot without signing.

## Layout

- `main.go`, `internal/cli/`: the command line and the MCP server
- `internal/spec/`: hakobu.toml
- `internal/seal/`: hakobu.secrets.toml
- `internal/server/`: the daemon: config, API, polling, monitoring
- `internal/apply/`: plans and deploys a release; watches the release images
- `internal/ci/`, `internal/scaffold/`: `hakobu build`/`wait`, `hakobu init` and the skill
- `internal/backups/`: sealed backups to S3, their proof and rotation
- `internal/alert/`, `internal/audit/`: email, pulse, the audit
- `internal/ingress/`: 80/443 with Let's Encrypt, or the tunnel's loopback
- `internal/node/`, `internal/deploy/`, `internal/proxy/`: Docker on the server, each app's proxy
- `internal/registry/`, `internal/status/`: the registry client, the commit status
